episode_title: The Ultimate Guide to B2B Product-Led Growth and Monetization
guest_role: Head of Growth at Dropbox, Amplitude, Miro advisor
content:
Lenny: Welcome Elena Verna. You are widely considered one of the foremost experts on B2B product-led growth (PLG). A lot of companies think PLG just means offering a free trial or a freemium plan. What are they misunderstanding?

Elena Verna: Offering a freemium plan is not PLG. Freemium is just a pricing strategy. True Product-Led Growth means the product itself is the primary driver of acquisition, retention, and monetization. In a traditional sales-led motion, humans (SDRs, AEs, CSMs) are doing the heavy lifting to find the customer, convince the customer, onboard them, and collect money. In PLG, the end-user self-serves through the product experience.

The most important concept people miss is the difference between an Acquisition Loop and a Sales Funnel. In a funnel, you pour traffic into the top and only a tiny percentage converts at the bottom. Once they convert, the funnel ends. In a Growth Loop, an action taken by a user generates an output that feeds back into new input. For example, in Miro or Dropbox, when user A creates a board and invites user B to collaborate, user B experiences the product and becomes user C who invites five more team members. That is a collaborative viral loop.

Lenny: How should companies think about when to gate features behind a paywall in B2B PLG?

Elena Verna: This is where most founders make critical mistakes. You have two types of paywalls: Usage-based paywalls and Feature-based paywalls.

Never put your core 'aha moment' behind a paywall. Your free tier must deliver fast, undeniable value to the single player. You want to get the user hooked on the daily habit loop. Once an individual user has formed an emotional attachment or workflow habit, you introduce gates around Collaboration, Security, Compliance, and Volume.

For example: single user is free; inviting a team or sharing externally triggers a team tier; SAML/SSO and audit logs trigger enterprise pricing. Enterprise buyers don't buy because of button color; they buy to manage risk, compliance, and centralized billing for software their teams are already addicted to using.
